An excellent choice for beginners and families, with night skiing and heliskiing options.
arkhyz.rating_basis: A modern resort with new gondolas and chairlifts, wide gentle runs and good service; skiresort.info test — 3.3 out of 5; heliskiing with EA Heli Skiing (January – March)
arkhyz.hazards: Avalanche danger off-piste, black ice and snowfall on the mountain road, strong sun at altitude; entering closed zones is prohibited
arkhyz.crowd_note: Over the New Year holidays and on February weekends, queues at the Mlechny Put lift and in the rental shops; quiet on weekdays
arkhyz.transfer: Mineralnye Vody ~210–220 km, 3–4.5 h (bus, transfer or taxi via Cherkessk)
pros: Modern lifts, well-groomed wide pistes
Great for beginners and families
Night skiing and a snowpark on the Southern slope
Heliskiing in the area (January – March)
Cheaper than Sochi
cons: Small ski area, few difficult runs
Unreliable snow early in the season (in 2025/26 the opening was pushed back to December)
Modest nightlife in Romantik
Long drive from Mineralnye Vody
arkhyz.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult: ~2550 ₽ early in the season and in spring, ~3250 ₽ in high season, up to 4050 ₽ at New Year and on peak dates in February–March (2024/25 prices; 2025/26 rates at resort-arkhyz.ru); night skiing ~1600–1950 ₽

dombay.description: A classic Karachay-Cherkessia resort in the Teberda Nature Reserve at the foot of Dombay-Ulgen. A new system of gondolas and chairlifts climbs to 3168 m on the slope of Mussa-Achitara, alongside old chairlifts and an aerial tramway. About 20–25 km of pistes and big freeride slopes with views of the Main Caucasus Range.
dombay.rating_basis: A legendary Soviet resort with stunning views of Dombay-Ulgen and good freeride; skiresort.info test — 3.0 out of 5; reviews criticise the scattered lifts run by different owners and poor control of avalanche-prone zones
dombay.hazards: High avalanche danger off-piste, poorly marked hazard zones; wind and frost on the exposed upper chairlifts; the Teberda – Dombay road is periodically closed due to avalanches and snowfall
dombay.crowd_note: Pistes are fairly busy in high season, especially around 2500 m; queues for the new gondola during holidays
dombay.region: Karachay-Cherkessia, Teberda National Park, Western Caucasus
dombay.season: December – late April; in snowy years the upper lifts (~3000 m) run until early May
dombay.transfer: Mineralnye Vody ~210–225 km, 3–3.5 h by car via Cherkessk and Teberda (transfer from ~7500 ₽ per car); bus to Teberda + taxi ~30 min
pros: One of Russia's most scenic resorts
Good freeride on the northern slopes of Mussa-Achitara
Over 1500 m of vertical, skiing up to ~3150 m
Affordable accommodation
cons: Lifts have different owners — different tickets
Upper chairlifts have no bubbles, cold and windy
No artificial snowmaking, little service
Long transfer from Mineralnye Vody, risk of the road being closed by avalanches
dombay.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, the new Dombay-1/2/3 system: 4400 ₽ over the New Year holidays and 1 Feb – 15 Mar, 3400 ₽ on 12–31 Jan and in the second half of March (per a howtrip review); other sources give 2400–2900 ₽; the old chairlifts and the aerial tramway need separate tickets

elbrus-azau.description: The slopes of Europe's highest mountain: cable cars climb from the Azau glade (2350 m) via Krugozor and Mir to Garabashi (3847 m), with snowcats going higher to the Pastukhov Rocks. 3 km away is the legendary Cheget, with steep untracked slopes and views of Elbrus. A region for advanced riders: altitude, wind and big freeride.
elbrus-azau.rating_basis: Europe's highest ski area (up to 3847 m) and, together with Cheget, Russia's main freeride region; skiresort.info test — 3.2 (Elbrus) and 2.9 (Cheget) out of 5 — the infrastructure lags behind Sochi
elbrus-azau.hazards: Altitude sickness and frostbite above 3500 m, strong wind and whiteouts, glacier crevasses off-piste, high avalanche danger on Cheget (north face only with a guide); along the Baksan gorge — risk of avalanches onto the road
elbrus-azau.crowd_note: Queues for the lower gondola in Azau over the New Year and March holidays; on Cheget — at the old chairlifts at weekends
elbrus-azau.season: late November – May; the upper slopes by Garabashi station (3800 m+) — until June
elbrus-azau.transfer: Nalchik airport ~120 km, ~2–2.5 h; Mineralnye Vody ~180 km, ~3–3.5 h (bus to Terskol via Nalchik, then a 10-min taxi)
pros: Europe's highest ski area — snow until May–June
World-class freeride and ski touring (Cheget, the Elbrus glaciers)
Lift pass prices low for the Caucasus
Views of Elbrus and the Main Caucasus Range
cons: Few runs for beginners, harsh conditions at altitude
Frequent wind closures of the upper sections
Old lifts on Cheget, modest infrastructure
Long drive from the airport, little nightlife
elbrus-azau.airport: NAL — Nalchik, ~2–2.5 h; MRV — Mineralnye Vody, ~3–3.5 h
elbrus-azau.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, Elbrus cable cars (Azau – Garabashi) — 3780 ₽, includes entry to Prielbrusye National Park; a day pass for Cheget — from ~1700 ₽ (separate pass)

gazprom-polyana.description: Gazprom's mountain resort in Esto-Sadok, with two areas: Laura — wide, gentle runs with night skiing, ideal for families and beginners — and Alpika — red and black runs from a 2256 m summit. The areas are linked by a 3S cable car, and at the base are the Polyana 1389 and Grand Hotel Polyana hotels.
gazprom-polyana.rating_basis: skiresort.info test — 3.2 out of 5; families and beginners praise Laura's wide, groomed, floodlit runs, while Alpika has red and black runs with over 1 km of vertical; freeride is officially banned
gazprom-polyana.hazards: Avalanche-prone slopes off-piste on Alpika (going there is prohibited), fog and wind up top, thaws and wet snow lower down in humid spells
gazprom-polyana.crowd_note: Usually quieter than Rosa Khutor (lift passes sold for 2+ days, many guests from the resort's own hotels); queues at the Laura gondola during holidays
gazprom-polyana.region: Krasnaya Polyana (Esto-Sadok), Sochi, Krasnodar Krai, Psekhako Ridge
gazprom-polyana.transfer: Sochi (Adler) airport: ~50 min by car (48 km), Lastochka train to Esto-Sadok/Gorki Gorod stations 30–60 min, buses 105, 105s, 535
pros: Excellent wide runs for beginners and families
Night skiing on Laura
Fewer people than Rosa Khutor
The Laura Olympic complex — cross-country skiing
cons: Lift passes mostly sold for 2+ days
Freeride is officially banned
Laura already closes in March
Little après-ski buzz in the areas themselves
gazprom-polyana.lift_pass_note: One-day passes are rarely on general sale: 2 days — from 8500 ₽ (≈4250 ₽/day), 3 days — from 9700 ₽; previously a day pass cost 4100 ₽; the combined pass with Rosa Khutor and Krasnaya Polyana — from 4800 ₽

kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.description: Kamchatka is one of the world's best places for heliskiing: descents from the Avachinsky, Koryaksky, Vilyuchinsky and Mutnovsky volcanoes down to the ocean, huge verticals and snow into summer. Lift-served skiing is modest: Moroznaya in Yelizovo (a chairlift and a T-bar, ~500 m vertical, snowmaking and floodlights), plus Edelweiss, Krasnaya Sopka and Kirpichiki in Petropavlovsk.
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.rating_basis: Rated as a heliskiing destination: runs down active volcanoes with up to 2000 m of vertical, 7000–10,000 m a day, snow until June (Powderhounds, Explore-Share tours); the ski bases themselves are small — skiresort.info test 2.9 (Moroznaya) and 2.3 (Edelweiss)
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.hazards: Active volcanoes (gas and ash emissions), strong cyclones, blizzards and no-fly weather, high avalanche danger and wind slabs, glacier crevasses; bears in spring; in February – March heavy snowfall and blizzards close the slopes
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.crowd_note: Practically no queues except at weekends on the town slopes; heliskiing is in small groups
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.region: Yelizovo and Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Kamchatka Krai, Russian Far East
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.season: pistes — December – April; volcano heliskiing — March – May (in places until June)
kamchatka-moroznaya-heliski.transfer: Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky (Yelizovo) airport — Moroznaya is a few minutes away by taxi; Petropavlovsk ~37 km, 40–50 min; heliskiing departs from helipads near Yelizovo/Paratunka
pros: World-class heliskiing on active volcanoes
Verticals up to 2000 m and 7000–10,000 m a day
A very long snow season — until May–June
No crowds, wild nature, Paratunka hot springs
cons: Lift-served bases are small and outdated
Very expensive heliskiing and flights (~9 h from Moscow)
Frequent no-fly days due to weather
Limited infrastructure and little service

kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.description: The Arctic's main resort, in the Khibiny above Kirovsk: about 27–30 km of pistes on the slopes of Aikuaivenchorr, gondolas and chairlifts, and 18 km of floodlit runs for skiing through the polar night and under the northern lights. Russia's longest season — from November to late May; nearby are Kukisvumchorr and Khibiny couloir freeride.
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.rating_basis: Russia's longest ski season (194 days and ~472,000 visitors in 2025/26) and skiing under the northern lights; skiresort.info test — 3.0 out of 5; downsides are wind, fog and the polar night in December
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.hazards: Strong wind, blizzards and whiteouts at the summit, Arctic air outbreaks (sudden severe frost), high avalanche danger in the Khibiny couloirs — off-piste only with a local guide
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.crowd_note: Peak load is the March holidays and spring (March – May), when people come from St Petersburg and Moscow; queues for the K6 gondola at weekends
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.region: Kirovsk, Murmansk Oblast, Khibiny, Kola Peninsula (Arctic)
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.season: mid/late November – late May (2025/26 season: 19 November – 31 May, 194 days)
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.transfer: Khibiny airport (Apatity) — taxi ~30 min, bus No. 130 40–60 min; Murmansk ~210 km, 2.5–3 h by car; train to Apatity (~1 day 8 h from Moscow) + 30–40 min by bus
pros: Season from November to late May — lots of sun and snow in spring
Skiing under the northern lights, floodlit runs
Khibiny freeride and ski touring in the couloirs
Easy to reach: Khibiny airport 30 min away
cons: Polar night in December, short daylight
Strong wind and fog close the upper lifts
Small vertical (~670 m)
Limited choice of restaurants and entertainment
kirovsk-bolshoy-vudyavr.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult: 2610 ₽ in high season, from 3420 ₽ on peak dates (New Year, March – May); 4 hours — from 1930 ₽

krasnaya-polyana-resort.description: The former Gornaya Karusel, on the northern slope of the Aibga Ridge, with its base station right in Gorki Gorod. About 30 km of pistes with ~1300 m of vertical, eight freeride zones below the Black Pyramid and in the cirques, two snowparks and night skiing; the season at the upper stations often lasts into May.
krasnaya-polyana-resort.rating_basis: skiresort.info test — 3.2 out of 5; valued for its 8 freeride zones (Black Pyramid, Cirque 2), two snowparks, night skiing and the Gorki Gorod village at the base station
krasnaya-polyana-resort.hazards: Serious avalanche danger in the freeride zones and cirques after snowfall, strong wind and fog at the upper stations; off-piste only with a guide and gear
krasnaya-polyana-resort.crowd_note: Queues for the K-1/K-2 gondolas over the New Year holidays and at weekends; noticeably quieter than Rosa Khutor on weekdays
krasnaya-polyana-resort.region: Esto-Sadok, Sochi, Krasnodar Krai, Aibga Ridge
krasnaya-polyana-resort.season: late December – early May (after the May holidays); the upper cirque sometimes runs longer
krasnaya-polyana-resort.transfer: Sochi (Adler) airport ~45 km: ~50 min by car, Lastochka train to Gorki Gorod (Esto-Sadok) station — from 30 min
pros: The best freeride terrain in Krasnaya Polyana (8 zones, steep cirques)
Long season up top — until May
Night skiing, two snowparks
The gondola starts by the Lastochka station and the Gorki Gorod mall
cons: Few gentle runs for beginners
Upper lifts often close due to wind and fog
Late season opening in low-snow years (26 December in 2025/26)
krasnaya-polyana-resort.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult: 3900 ₽ until 28 December and in April–May, 5250 ₽ over the New Year dates 28 Dec – 11 Jan; evening pass — 2100/3200 ₽; children under 6 — 1 ₽

manzherok.description: A modern resort on the slopes of Mount Malaya Sinyukha by the Chuysky Trakt in the Altai Republic: about 50 km of pistes, a gondola and high-speed chairlifts, ~850 m of vertical and the longest green run, Argut (~5.5 km). Aimed at families and beginners, with a snowpark, night skiing and five après-ski venues. Neighbouring Belokurikha (Altai Krai) is a smaller resort-spa.
manzherok.rating_basis: Sber's new year-round resort with ~50 km of pistes and a gondola — the largest in Siberia by piste length; skiresort.info test — 3.4 out of 5; almost no freeride
manzherok.hazards: Severe frost in December – January, wind on the Sinyukha summit; off-piste — forest and steep slopes, low avalanche danger
manzherok.crowd_note: Busy over the New Year holidays and at weekends (close to Barnaul and Novosibirsk), quiet on weekdays
manzherok.region: Mayminsky District, Altai Republic, Mount Malaya Sinyukha
manzherok.season: late November/December – late March to mid-April (partial opening on 16 November in 2025/26)
manzherok.transfer: Gorno-Altaysk airport 30–40 min along the Chuysky Trakt; Barnaul ~4 h, Novosibirsk ~6–7 h by car
pros: ~50 km of pistes — one of Siberia's largest resorts
New lifts, wide runs for beginners
Children under 10 ski free
Gorno-Altaysk airport 40 minutes away
cons: Low mountain: few difficult runs and almost no freeride
Unreliable snow lower down early in the season
Frost in January
The season ends as early as early to mid-April
manzherok.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult — 2800–3000 ₽ (sources vary), children under 10 — free; evening pass — 1700 ₽, day + evening — 3600 ₽

rosa-khutor.description: Russia's main ski resort and the 2014 Olympic mountain, on the Aibga Ridge: about 100 km of pistes, more than 1500 m of vertical, modern gondolas and the large resort village of Rosa Dolina on the banks of the Mzymta. It suits everyone — from beginners on the southern slope to freeriders in the northern cirques.
rosa-khutor.rating_basis: Russia's largest and most visited resort (≈100 km of pistes, 2014 Olympic venues); skiresort.info test — 3.6 out of 5, 4 out of 5 for advanced/freeride — the best in southern Russia
rosa-khutor.hazards: High avalanche danger off-piste after snowfall (heavy precipitation from the Black Sea), fog and wind closures of the upper lifts; freeride only with a guide and avalanche gear
rosa-khutor.crowd_note: Very busy over the New Year holidays and on February weekends: queues for the lower gondolas and at the Rosa Plateau; quieter on weekdays in January and March
rosa-khutor.region: Krasnaya Polyana, Sochi, Krasnodar Krai, Western Caucasus
rosa-khutor.season: mid-December – mid/late April (lifts run from early December)
rosa-khutor.transfer: Sochi (Adler) airport ~50 km: ~50–60 min by car/taxi, Lastochka train to Rosa Khutor station ~1 h, buses 105/535 ~1.5 h
pros: Russia's largest ski area, ~1.5 km of vertical
Modern gondolas and chairlifts, powerful snowmaking (400+ snow guns)
Olympic extreme park, several snowparks
Freeride descents in the northern cirques of the Aibga Ridge
Well-developed infrastructure, hotels and restaurants in the village, a direct train from the airport
cons: Expensive lift passes and accommodation by Russian standards
Queues during holidays and weekends
Humid maritime climate: thaws, fog, heavy snow lower down
The lower runs turn slushy quickly in spring
rosa-khutor.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, Rosa Khutor only — 6350 ₽ (per ski.ru); dynamic pricing: 4850–6500 ₽ depending on dates in the 2024/25 season; the combined pass for the Krasnaya Polyana resorts in 2025/26 — 5800–7700 ₽

sheregesh.description: Siberia's main ski resort, on Mount Zelyonaya in Gornaya Shoria: several sectors (A, V, E, F) run by different operators, about 40 km of pistes and over 20 lifts. Famous for huge amounts of dry powder, tree freeride and fun parties like the Grelka festival.
sheregesh.rating_basis: Siberia's most popular resort and Russia's top powder resort: dry snow up to 2–4 m deep, tree freeride and cat-skiing tours; downsides are several operators with different passes and severe frost
sheregesh.hazards: Severe frost and wind on the Zelyonaya summit (frostbite), fog and poor visibility; in the freeride zones — avalanche-prone slopes, trees and unfrozen streams in the gullies; go off-piste only with a guide and a transceiver
sheregesh.crowd_note: Queues for the central lifts at weekends, over the New Year holidays and during the Grelka festival in April; quieter on weekdays in late November and March
sheregesh.region: Tashtagolsky District, Kemerovo Oblast – Kuzbass, Gornaya Shoria
sheregesh.season: late November – late April (off-piste powder freeride from about mid-December)
sheregesh.transfer: Novokuznetsk (Spichenkovo) airport ~160 km, 2.5–3 h by transfer (minivan ~7000 ₽ per vehicle); Kemerovo airport ~400 km, ~5–6 h
pros: Lots of dry snow — Russia's best powder
Excellent tree freeride and cat-skiing tours
Long season from late November to late April
Night skiing, snowpark in sector E
Party atmosphere, the spring Grelka festival
cons: Severe frost in December–January (down to −30…−35 °C)
Fragmented: different operators and passes, the combined one costs more
Small vertical (~700 m)
A long trip — a flight to Novokuznetsk plus 3 h by road
sheregesh.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, the “Combined” pass for 19 lifts of different operators — 4250 ₽; single-sector passes are cheaper (Kaskad — 3200 ₽, Sector E — 3100 ₽), evening pass — 1700 ₽

sobolinaya-baikalsk.description: A resort on the slopes of the Khamar-Daban above Baikalsk, with views of Lake Baikal: 18 runs totalling about 15 km, ~480 m of vertical, a chairlift and T-bars. Famous for abundant dry snow, steep ungroomed runs (Prezidentskaya, Mogul) and tree skiing.
sobolinaya-baikalsk.rating_basis: The Baikal region's main resort: snowy Khamar-Daban, tree and steep ungroomed runs with views of Baikal; skiresort.info test — 2.7 out of 5; old infrastructure
sobolinaya-baikalsk.hazards: Frost below −20 °C in January, morning ice and slushy snow in spring, poor visibility; avalanche danger on ungroomed slopes after snowfall; Baikal's ice is dangerous without proven routes
sobolinaya-baikalsk.crowd_note: Busy over the New Year holidays and at weekends (visitors from Irkutsk), the runs are almost empty on weekdays
sobolinaya-baikalsk.region: Baikalsk, Irkutsk Oblast, Khamar-Daban Range, southern shore of Lake Baikal
sobolinaya-baikalsk.season: mid-December – second half of April (2025/26: 13 December – 25 April)
sobolinaya-baikalsk.transfer: Irkutsk ~140 km: ~2–2.5 h by car, ~4 h by bus or train to Baikalsk, then taxi
pros: Lots of snow — Khamar-Daban is one of the snowiest places in Siberia
Views of Baikal from the top
Steep and tree runs for advanced riders
Inexpensive lift pass
cons: Outdated lifts (mostly T-bars)
Severe frost in January
Modest infrastructure and nightlife
Far from Irkutsk
sobolinaya-baikalsk.lift_pass_note: 1 day (10:00–17:00), adult: weekdays — 1800 ₽, weekends — 2700 ₽; more on holidays; skiresort.info gives 3600 ₽ (season not specified)

are.description: Scandinavia's largest and best-known ski resort, on the slopes of Åreskutan: about 90 km of pistes, almost 1000 m of vertical and several linked areas (Åre By, Tegefjäll, Duved, Björnen). A World Cup resort with a lively village right by the railway station and the best après-ski in Sweden. In spring — long sunny days and deep snow.
are.rating_basis: skiresort.com test — 4.2/5 (“Outstanding”): snow, families, beginners, snowpark, après-ski; Scandinavia's largest resort, World Cup races and Alpine World Ski Championships
are.hazards: Strong wind and frost on the Åreskutan summit (the upper lifts are often closed), whiteouts and poor visibility above the treeline, avalanche danger off-piste (Ullådalen, the Åreskutan couloirs), frostbite in January.
are.crowd_note: Peak times are the Swedish sports holidays (February, weeks 7–10) and Easter: queues at the Kabinbanan and VM8:an; quiet in January and on weekdays in March
are.season: late November / early December – early May (best in February – April)
are.transfer: Östersund ~1 h (100 km), Trondheim (Norway) ~2–2.5 h, direct train from Stockholm ~6–7 h to the station in central Åre
pros: Scandinavia's biggest area and vertical
Long season until early May, excellent spring snow
Lively après-ski, a village with a railway station by the lifts
Good conditions for families, night skiing
cons: Expensive: accommodation, food, lift pass
Short daylight and severe frost in December–January
The top is often closed due to wind
Few black runs
are.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, main season — 801 SEK (≈€72) per skiresort.com; SkiStar uses dynamic pricing, 755 SEK in the 2024/25 season

jasna.description: Slovakia's largest ski resort, on both sides of Chopok (2004 m): the northern Jasná side with steep runs and Chopok South, linked by gondolas. The region's best freeride and snowpark, modern lifts and more than 1000 m of vertical. A cheaper alternative to the Alps, though nightlife is mostly in the hotels.
jasna.rating_basis: skiresort.com test — 4.0/5 (“Very good”): freeride, restaurants, pistes, lifts, snow; the largest resort in Slovakia and in Eastern Europe outside the Alps, Freeride World Qualifier events
jasna.hazards: Strong wind on the Chopok ridge (frequent closures of the upper gondolas), fog and icing, avalanche danger off-piste in the couloirs and on Chopok South; the HZS mountain rescue service requires you to follow the freeride zone rules.
jasna.crowd_note: Busy at weekends and during the Czech, Polish and Hungarian school holidays (February); quiet on weekdays
jasna.season: early December – late April (on Chopok sometimes until 1 May)
jasna.transfer: Poprad-Tatry ~1–1.25 h (≈60 km), Košice ~2 h, Kraków ~3 h, Bratislava ~3.5 h, Vienna ~4 h; the nearest railway station is Liptovský Mikuláš (≈15 km, ski bus)
pros: The best freeride and terrain in Central Europe outside the Alps
Modern gondolas, north and south sides of the mountain
Good snowmaking, season until late April
Prices lower than in the Alps
cons: Low summit (2004 m) — the top is often in wind and fog
The ticket-office lift pass costs almost as much as in the Alps
Après-ski mostly in the hotels
Weekend traffic jams and queues
jasna.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult, main season — €71 (ticket office); noticeably cheaper when bought online in advance via GOPASS, dynamic pricing

erciyes.description: Turkey's main ski resort, on the slopes of the extinct Erciyes volcano: wide treeless slopes with about 1250 m of vertical, new lifts and four entry points (Tekir, Hisarcık, Develi, Hacılar). Dry snow, lots of sun and beginner-friendly freeride; Cappadocia is nearby. The resort claims 100+ km of pistes, skiresort.com counts ~55 km. The alternative in eastern Turkey is Palandöken (Erzurum): 43 km of pistes up to 3140 m, even drier and colder.
erciyes.rating_basis: skiresort.com test — 3.5/5 (“Very good”); Turkey's largest and most modern resort (>3 million visitors a season), the slopes of an extinct volcano up to 3346 m
erciyes.hazards: Strong wind and blizzards on the volcano's open slopes (upper-lift closures), altitude above 3000 m, strong sun, wind-hardened snow; avalanche danger is generally low but possible off-piste and in the couloirs below the summit.
erciyes.crowd_note: Very busy during the Turkish winter school holidays (sömestr, late January – early February) and at weekends — hundreds of thousands of visitors; quiet on weekdays in December and March
erciyes.season: early December – early April (in snowy years until late April)
erciyes.transfer: Kayseri ~30–40 min (≈25 km; taxi ~€20), Cappadocia (Nevşehir) ~1.5 h
pros: ~1250 m vertical and altitude up to 3346 m
Dry snow and wide open freeride terrain
Airport 30–40 minutes away, Cappadocia nearby
Inexpensive, no visa for Russians
cons: Instructors mostly speak Turkish and English, rarely Russian
Crowds during the Turkish school holidays
Almost no après-ski (alcohol only in hotels)
Strong wind on the treeless slopes
erciyes.lift_pass_note: Full day — 950 TL (≈€25) in the 2024/25 season; in 2025/26 the resort also sells passes by number of rides (1 ride — 90 TL), with a 50% discount at the Hacılar and Hisarcık gates. Lira prices are rising fast due to inflation

uludag.description: Turkey's oldest and best-known ski resort, above Bursa — the “Mysian Olympus”. The hotels stand right on the slopes in the Oteller area; the runs are mostly short, with some difficult ones. Popular with Istanbulites for weekends: noisy hotels with nightlife, but queues and a mixed bag of lifts.
uludag.rating_basis: skiresort.com test — 3.1/5 (“Good”): the closest major resort to Istanbul, one of Turkey's largest areas, but the lifts are a mixed bag and the runs are scattered
uludag.hazards: Fog and blizzards (frequent on Uludağ), strong wind, ice during thaws, traffic jams and black ice on the mountain road from Bursa.
uludag.crowd_note: Very busy at weekends (Istanbulites) and during the Turkish school holidays (late January – early February); noticeably quieter on weekdays
uludag.transfer: Bursa ~1 h (≈35 km; or the Teleferik cable car from Bursa to Sarıalan + shuttle), Istanbul ~3–3.5 h, Bursa Yenişehir airport ~1.5 h
pros: Close to Istanbul and Bursa
Ski-in/ski-out hotels in the Oteller area
Lively nightlife in the hotels
No visa for Russians
cons: Small vertical (~540 m) and short runs
Crowds at weekends and during school holidays
Unreliable snow in warm winters
Lifts with different owners, outdated infrastructure
uludag.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult: ticket office 1,500 TL, online 1,400 TL (≈€30); lira prices are rising fast due to inflation

jackson-hole.description: A freeride legend in the Rockies: ~1260 m of vertical, almost half the terrain black and double-black runs, couloirs (Corbet's Couloir), cliffs and gate access to the vast Teton backcountry; heliskiing too. Teton Village sits at the base, and the cowboy town of Jackson, 20 km away, has bars and restaurants. Dry continental snow, but it's cold.
jackson-hole.rating_basis: skiresort.com — 4.2/5 (“Outstanding”); a cult resort for experts — Corbet's Couloir, the Tram, often No. 1 in SKI Magazine rankings for challenging terrain
jackson-hole.hazards: Avalanche danger in the Teton backcountry (only with gear and a guide), steep couloirs and cliffs, severe frost and wind at the summit (3185 m), tree wells
jackson-hole.crowd_note: Long queue for the Tram on powder mornings and holidays; bearable on the other lifts
jackson-hole.season: late November / early December – early April
jackson-hole.transfer: Jackson Hole airport (JAC) ~30–40 min; Idaho Falls (IDA) ~2.5 h; Salt Lake City (SLC) ~5 h
pros: Some of the best extreme terrain in the US
Backcountry access through gates, heliskiing
Dry snow and big vertical
Wild West atmosphere and national parks nearby
cons: Few easy runs for beginners
Expensive lift pass and accommodation
Severe frost and wind
Far from major hubs
jackson-hole.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult — price depends on the date: sample 2025/26 mid-season prices — $225 on weekdays, $285 at weekends; more at the ticket office on peak dates (skiresort.com — $304). Included in the Ikon Pass

mammoth-mountain.description: California's largest resort, on the slopes of an extinct volcano: ~950 m of vertical, open bowls and couloirs near the 3369 m summit and the famous Unbound parks with a halfpipe. Pacific storms bring huge amounts of snow, so the season runs from November to June, and in record years into summer; in spring people ski in T-shirts. The town of Mammoth Lakes below has restaurants, plus a village with a gondola.
mammoth-mountain.rating_basis: skiresort.com — 4.4/5 (“Outstanding”); one of the snowiest and longest seasons in the US, the famous Unbound parks
mammoth-mountain.hazards: Altitude 2400–3400 m (altitude sickness), hurricane-force wind near the summit, avalanche danger in the couloirs after storms, volcanic gases in some hollows off-piste
mammoth-mountain.crowd_note: Lots of skiers from Los Angeles at weekends and holidays, queues at Main Lodge; quiet on weekdays and in spring
mammoth-mountain.season: early/mid-November – early June (in big snow years until July or even early August)
mammoth-mountain.transfer: Local Mammoth Yosemite airport (MMH) ~15 min (few flights); Reno (RNO) ~3 h; Los Angeles ~5–6 h by car
pros: Very long season — skiing in May–June
Lots of snow and sunny days
World-class parks and halfpipe
Steep couloirs near the summit
cons: Heavy, wet snow (“Sierra cement”) after storms
Strong wind closes the upper lifts
Weekend crowds from Los Angeles
Far from major airports
mammoth-mountain.airport: RNO — Reno, ~3 h (MMH — Mammoth Lakes, ~15 min)
mammoth-mountain.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult — dynamic price: a sample online mid-season price for 2025/26 is $189; more on holidays and at the ticket office (skiresort.com — $259). Included in the Ikon Pass

vail.description: One of the largest and best-known resorts in the US: about 5300 acres (~2150 ha) of terrain, a front side with groomed runs and the famous Back Bowls and Blue Sky Basin — huge open bowls and trees for powder lovers. A Tyrolean-style village with pricey hotels, restaurants and lively après-ski. Dry Colorado snow and sun, but the base sits at ~2500 m.
vail.rating_basis: skiresort.com — 4.5/5 (“Outstanding”); the Vail Resorts flagship, consistently near the top of SKI Magazine rankings; ~2150 ha of terrain
vail.hazards: Altitude (altitude sickness, dehydration), severe frost in January, avalanche danger beyond the resort boundary; I-70 closures during snowfall
vail.crowd_note: On holidays and at weekends (Denver locals on I-70) queues at the village gondolas and the Back Bowls lifts; better on weekdays in January and early March
vail.transfer: Eagle County (EGE) ~40 min; Denver (DEN) ~2–2.5 h via I-70 (~190 km, longer in snowfall)
pros: Huge terrain: Back Bowls and Blue Sky Basin
Dry snow and lots of sunny days
Excellent infrastructure and après-ski
Good for all levels
cons: One of the most expensive lift passes in the world (an Epic Pass is better value)
Crowds at weekends and holidays
Altitude 2500–3500 m — risk of altitude sickness
Little truly steep terrain
vail.lift_pass_note: 1 day, adult — dynamic price: sample 2025/26 online prices are $307 on weekdays and $335 at weekends; more at the ticket office on holidays (skiresort.com — $356). Much cheaper with an Epic Pass / Epic Day Pass bought in advance

amirsoy.description: A modern resort in the Chimgan Mountains, an hour and a half from Tashkent: gondolas, snowmaking, about 16 km of pistes with ~660 m of vertical and luxury chalets at the base station. Excellent for beginners and families; advanced riders get off-piste terrain on the ridges, ski touring and inexpensive heliskiing around Chimgan and Beldersay.
amirsoy.rating_basis: Uzbekistan's first modern resort (opened in 2019): new gondolas, TechnoAlpin snowmaking, chalet hotels; skiresort.info test — 3.1 out of 5; the runs are easy, but there's good off-piste terrain nearby and inexpensive heliskiing in Chimgan (Powderhounds)
amirsoy.hazards: Avalanche danger on Chimgan's off-piste slopes after snowfall, rapid warming and wet snow in spring, fog; black ice on the road from Tashkent
amirsoy.crowd_note: Lots of visitors from Tashkent at weekends and holidays (including sightseers on the gondola), quiet on weekdays
amirsoy.region: Bostanliq District, Tashkent Region, Western Tian Shan (Chimgan Mountains)
amirsoy.season: mid-December – late March (with snowmaking possibly from late November)
amirsoy.transfer: Tashkent airport ~65–80 km, ~1.5 h by car/taxi
pros: New gondolas and snowmaking
Visa-free for Russians, everyone understands Russian
Great for beginners and families
Inexpensive heliskiing and ski touring in Chimgan nearby
cons: Small ski area, no black runs
Short season on low slopes — unreliable snow in December and March
Expensive chalet accommodation, little nightlife
Gondola queues at weekends
amirsoy.lift_pass_note: 1 day (09:00–16:00), adult: weekdays — 320,000 som, weekends (Fri–Sun and holidays) — 390,000 som; half day — 240,000/290,000 som; beginner pass — 190,000/250,000 som

noravank-yeghegnadzor.description: The canyons of Vayots Dzor around Areni, Noravank and Yeghegnadzor are Armenia's main sport climbing area. Compact limestone on red and grey walls, routes from 5 to 7c and a couple of ~150 m multi-pitches in the Noravank gorge and the Jokhk Dzor gorge (“Hell's Canyon”). The Noravank and Tatev monasteries and the Areni wineries are close by — a good option for combining climbing with travel.
noravank-yeghegnadzor.rating_basis: Armenia's main sport climbing area (the whole country has ~100 sport routes 5–7c), beautiful canyons and monasteries; little information and few routes
noravank-yeghegnadzor.hazards: Heat and sun in summer, loose rock on rarely climbed routes, snakes
noravank-yeghegnadzor.crowd_note: Mostly local climbers and the occasional group — usually empty
noravank-yeghegnadzor.region: Vayots Dzor; Noravank, Areni and Jokhk Dzor canyons
noravank-yeghegnadzor.season: April–May and September–October; hot in summer, cold in winter
noravank-yeghegnadzor.transfer: ~2 h by car from Yerevan (~110–120 km) on the highway south via Ararat and Areni
noravank-yeghegnadzor.rock_note: compact limestone in the Areni and Noravank canyons: red and grey walls, a cave, a few multi-pitches of around 150 m; Jokhk Dzor gorge (“Hell's Canyon”) has walls up to ~200 m
noravank-yeghegnadzor.approach: Sectors along the roads in the Noravank and Jokhk Dzor canyons, short approaches
noravank-yeghegnadzor.stay: Guesthouses in Yeghegnadzor and Areni; campsites around Goris
pros: Beautiful canyons and monasteries
Empty and inexpensive
Russian widely understood
Areni wine and food
cons: Few routes and little information, no guidebook
Few hard routes
Hot summers
school_notes: Spring (April–May) and autumn climbing camps: Jokhk Dzor, Noravank, Goris; transfers, guesthouses and group gear rental included

frey-bariloche.description: A cirque of granite spires above the mountain lake Laguna Toncek in the Cerro Catedral massif — Argentina's top trad destination, with the feel of a miniature Patagonia. Hundreds of crack routes of 1–8 pitches topping out on tiny summits, with the cosy Refugio Frey, serving dinners and beer, as your base. Climbing is possible only in the southern summer.
frey-bariloche.rating_basis: Argentina's best-known granite area: over 300 routes according to ClimbingAway, ~120 on Mountain Project; a unique alpine setting with a hut among the spires, but a short season, a long approach and difficult weather
frey-bariloche.hazards: Strong winds and sudden weather changes, snow even in summer, scree and rockfall on the approaches, tábano horseflies in January, long rappels (two ropes needed); rescue is by Club Andino volunteers only
frey-bariloche.crowd_note: In January–February (Argentine summer holidays) the hut and campsite are full of trekkers and there can be queues on the Aguja Frey classics; the more distant spires are quiet
frey-bariloche.region: Río Negro, Northern Patagonia, Nahuel Huapi National Park, Cerro Catedral massif above Bariloche
frey-bariloche.season: December–March (southern summer), February is the driest month; November and April depend on the weather, with possible snow and cold wind; May to October is winter (Cerro Catedral runs as a ski resort)
frey-bariloche.transfer: Fly to Bariloche (~2 h from Buenos Aires), take city bus 55P to Villa Catedral, then walk; porters can be hired through Club Andino
frey-bariloche.rock_note: pale, coarse-grained granite on more than 30 spires and towers 20–250 m high in the cirque above Laguna Toncek: cracks, dihedrals, arêtes and slabs, routes of 1–8 pitches topping out on small summits
frey-bariloche.approach: There is no road to Refugio Frey: bus 55P from Bariloche to Villa Catedral (~40 min), then 3–5 h on foot (10.5 km, +750 m), or ride the lift and walk ~3 h along the Filo de Catedral ridge; from the hut to the spires is 5 min to 3 h over scree
frey-bariloche.restrictions: Nahuel Huapi National Park: camping by the hut requires a free trekking permit and an online booking (no more than 3 days ahead, up to 5 nights, extendable); campfires are prohibited, use the hut's toilets. Old-school ethics: bolts only as a last resort; many anchors and old bolts are rusty or homemade.
frey-bariloche.guidebook: Topo sold at Refugio Frey (Club Andino Bariloche)
frey-bariloche.stay: Refugio Emilio Frey (Club Andino Bariloche): bunks, dinners, beer and snacks, large cams sometimes for rent; free camping by Laguna Toncek (booking required, winds can exceed 50 km/h); hostels and hotels in Bariloche
pros: Stunning granite spires in an alpine cirque
Cosy hut and free camping right by the rock
Classic mid-grade crack climbing
Bariloche nearby — easy to reach from Buenos Aires
cons: Long walk-in, carrying all your gear
Short season and fickle Patagonian weather
Few sport routes, old bolts
No phone signal and no gear rental on site
frey-bariloche.airport: BRC — San Carlos de Bariloche, ~30 min to Villa Catedral + 3–5 h on foot
famous_lines: Objetivo Luna 5.10c (6b), 8 pitches, El Cohete Lunar
school_notes: Programs by local Bariloche guides on the Explore-Share platform
Gear placement and anchor-building instruction for trad beginners

arapiles-dyurrite.description: Arapiles (Dyurrite) is a lone sandstone mountain rising from the Wimmera wheat fields and arguably the best trad area in the Southern Hemisphere: thousands of routes on perfect gear-protected cracks, from easy lines to the historic Punks in the Gym. The village of Natimuk lives for climbers, and most walls are a couple of minutes from the campground. Cultural heritage closures have been in force since the 2020s, and a new management plan is still under discussion.
arapiles-dyurrite.rating_basis: Australia's legendary trad area: 2,000+ quality routes (chockstone.org) on a small mountain; Punks in the Gym is the historic first 8b+; the downside is the growing number of closures
arapiles-dyurrite.hazards: Heat and sun in summer, fire danger, snakes, falls on poorly protected trad routes, polished holds
arapiles-dyurrite.crowd_note: At Easter the campground and the classic walls are packed, with queues at the Organ Pipes; quiet on weekdays
arapiles-dyurrite.region: Victoria, Wimmera, Natimuk — Mount Arapiles-Tooan State Park
arapiles-dyurrite.season: year-round, best in March–May and October–November; hot in summer (climb in the shade and in the morning), cool in winter but drier than the Grampians
arapiles-dyurrite.transfer: ~4 h by car from Melbourne (≈300 km) via Horsham; or train to Ararat, V/Line bus to Horsham and a local bus to Natimuk
arapiles-dyurrite.rock_note: very solid quartzite sandstone: perfect cracks for gear, roofs, “organ pipes”; the classics are polished
arapiles-dyurrite.approach: Most walls are 2–15 min on foot from The Pines campground
arapiles-dyurrite.restrictions: Some sectors are closed to protect Aboriginal cultural heritage (Declaration Crag, Tiger Wall, Castle Crag and others). The draft Dyurrite management plan (2024) proposes closing about half the routes (The Pharos, Yesterday Gully, Mitre Rock, Tiptoe Ridge) and The Pines campground while keeping ~80 areas open; the plan is being finalised in 2025–2026 — check with Parks Victoria before your trip. From 1 November to 30 April gas stoves only, no campfires; trad ethics, and the few bolts have no hangers (bring bolt plates)
arapiles-dyurrite.guidebook: Arapiles guidebooks are sold at the shop in Natimuk; online topos on theCrag and chockstone.org
arapiles-dyurrite.stay: The Pines campground at the foot of the mountain (book online; may close under the new plan), houses and rooms in Natimuk — a climbers' village with a pub and a gear shop
pros: Huge choice of trad at every grade
Great place to learn trad
Rock minutes from the campground
Dry climate — climbable almost all year
cons: Closures and uncertainty over the management plan
Polished classics
Summer heat and fire restrictions
Far from Melbourne
famous_lines: Punks in the Gym 8b+ (Ewbank 31–32, the world's first 8b+, Güllich 1985)
school_notes: Official register of licensed guides in Victoria; local schools and a shop with gear rental operate in Natimuk

blue-mountains.description: The Blue Mountains are a sandstone plateau west of Sydney with endless cliffs above eucalyptus gorges. Thousands of routes, mostly single-pitch sport on steep walls with small holds, plus trad and multi-pitches — all within one to two hours of the city. The bases are Blackheath, Katoomba and Mount Victoria.
blue-mountains.rating_basis: The state's largest area: over 5,000 routes (Mountain Project) on 45+ crags (ClimbingAway), quality sandstone sport climbing 2 hours from Sydney
blue-mountains.hazards: Bushfires and total fire bans, snakes and leeches, flies, rockfall from the cliffs, sudden weather changes on the plateau
blue-mountains.crowd_note: At weekends the popular sport crags around Blackheath fill up with Sydneysiders; quiet on weekdays
blue-mountains.season: March–May and September–November; hot and humid in summer (climb in the shady gorges), cold in winter — pick sunny walls
blue-mountains.transfer: ~1.5–2 h from Sydney by car on the Great Western Highway, or by train to Katoomba / Blackheath
blue-mountains.rock_note: orange sandstone on the plateau's sheer cliffs: steep, slightly overhanging walls with small holds, and in places long multi-pitches up to 120 m
blue-mountains.approach: Drive to the cliff edge, then 5–30 min on foot down to the crags (and back uphill)
blue-mountains.restrictions: Most crags are in Blue Mountains National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage site) and subject to NPWS rules; some sectors are on private land with their own access conditions (see the guidebook); don't climb on wet sandstone; fire bans and closures apply during periods of fire danger
blue-mountains.guidebook: Best of the Blue (sport); Blue Mountains Selected Sport Climbs; online topo on theCrag
blue-mountains.stay: Guesthouses, hostels and motels in Blackheath, Katoomba and Mount Victoria; national park campsites
pros: Thousands of routes near Sydney
Excellent mid- and high-grade sport
Reachable by train
Crags in both shade and sun
cons: Flies and mosquitoes in summer
Sandstone can't be climbed when wet
Some crags are hard to find without a guidebook
school_notes: Climbing courses and guides in Katoomba
Beginner courses, abseiling

grampians-gariwerd.description: The Grampians (Gariwerd) are sandstone ranges in western Victoria and a world-class area: the pocketed Taipan Wall with routes up to 8c+, overhanging caves, trad and long multi-pitches, and the legendary boulder Wheel of Life. Since 2019 climbing has been allowed only in officially designated areas, which are gradually being reopened after surveys carried out together with the Traditional Owners.
grampians-gariwerd.rating_basis: One of the world's best areas for sandstone quality: 4,800+ routes (chockstone.org), Taipan Wall and the caves of the Northern Grampians; rating lowered because of the sweeping closures since 2019
grampians-gariwerd.hazards: Heat, bushfires and total fire bans, snakes (tiger snake, brown snake), rockfall on multi-pitches, sudden bad weather in winter
grampians-gariwerd.crowd_note: At Easter and on long weekends Stapylton campground is overflowing and there are queues on the open classic walls
grampians-gariwerd.region: Victoria, Grampians National Park, Halls Gap
grampians-gariwerd.season: March–May and October–November; summer brings heat and fire danger (climb early in the morning and in the shade); winter is cool and rainy — climbers head for sunny walls and the caves
grampians-gariwerd.transfer: ~3–3.5 h by car from Melbourne (≈260 km) to Halls Gap; a car is essential
grampians-gariwerd.rock_note: hard orange-grey sandstone: smooth walls with “bullet-hole” pockets (Taipan Wall), overhanging caves, cracks and long multi-pitches
grampians-gariwerd.approach: From 5 min to 1.5 h; Taipan Wall is ~20 min uphill from Stapylton campground; some sectors require a 4WD
grampians-gariwerd.restrictions: Climbing is allowed ONLY in Parks Victoria's official designated climbing areas — everything else has been closed to protect Aboriginal cultural heritage (since 2019). 18 areas reopened in May 2025 and another 17 in June 2026 (500+ routes); Spurt Wall is closed, Taipan Wall is partly open (some routes closed or with a new approach), Tortoise Wall has been temporarily closed since April 2026, Centurion Walls partly. Bouldering only in a few designated zones (e.g. Andersens West), and no new ones will be added. Summer Day Valley only with a licensed operator. A mandatory free online permit is in preparation. Use minimal chalk, coloured to match the rock; the park closes on total fire ban days and during fires
grampians-gariwerd.guidebook: Online topos on theCrag and chockstone.org; local Grampians guidebooks; current maps of the open areas on the Parks Victoria website (check before your trip)
grampians-gariwerd.stay: 14 official park campgrounds (the best for climbers is Stapylton, with water, near Taipan and Hollow Mountain), motels and cottages in Halls Gap
pros: World-class sandstone, the legendary Taipan Wall
Huge range of styles: sport, trad, multi-pitch
Campgrounds right by the rock
Climbable almost all year
cons: Sweeping closures, rules change often
Almost all bouldering is closed
Summer heat and fires
Car needed, far from Melbourne
famous_lines: Passport to Insanity 7c (Ewbank 27, The Fortress, 135 m)
Wheel of Life 8C (boulder, Hollow Mountain Cave — check access status)
school_notes: Official list of licensed guides and schools in the park

vratsa.description: Vratsa is Bulgaria's main climbing area, in the Vratsata gorge in the Balkan foothills, 110 km from Sofia. About 580 routes: ~250 sport routes 5c–8c and long trad and alpine routes up to 400 m on the Central Wall — the biggest in the country. Other areas are close by too: Lakatnik and Karlukovo.
vratsa.rating_basis: Bulgaria's largest climbing area: 580+ routes and the country's biggest wall (up to 400 m); known mainly to local and Balkan climbers
vratsa.hazards: Loose rock, especially on multi-pitches; old protection on trad routes
vratsa.crowd_note: Climbers from Sofia come at weekends; quiet on weekdays
vratsa.region: Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park, Vratsata gorge
vratsa.season: Spring and autumn (April–June, September–October); shady sectors in summer; cold in winter
vratsa.transfer: ~110 km (≈1.5–2 h) by car from Sofia; trains and buses run to Vratsa, then a taxi from town to the gorge
vratsa.rock_note: limestone of the Vratsata gorge: the Central Wall, up to 400 m, is the biggest in Bulgaria; sport sectors on vertical and overhanging rock
vratsa.approach: 5–20 min from the parking in the Vratsata gorge to the sport sectors; a short approach from the road to the Central Wall
vratsa.restrictions: Most crags lie within the protected Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park: developing new crags is not allowed (new routes on existing ones are), and the Zgorigradska wall is closed to climbing; littering and chipping holds are not tolerated
vratsa.guidebook: Vratsa Climbing Guide, 2nd ed. 2020: 583 routes (~250 sport, the rest trad / alpine multi-pitches up to 350 m); online databases climbingguidebg.com and theCrag
vratsa.stay: Hotels and guesthouses in the town of Vratsa, 2–3 km from the gorge
pros: Bulgaria's biggest wall, long multi-pitches
Inexpensive, few people
Close to Sofia
cons: Few easy sport routes
Chossy rock in places
Cold winters
school_notes: Guided ascents of the Vratsa Central Wall, programs for beginners and experienced climbers
Bulgarian school running trips to Vratsa
Outdoor rock climbing course

rio-de-janeiro-urca.description: One of the world's best urban climbing destinations: the granite-gneiss domes of Sugarloaf, Urca and Corcovado rise straight out of the city and the ocean. The classics are multi-pitch slab and face routes with sparse bolts and summit views over Guanabara Bay, plus short sport crags (“falésias”) around the city.
rio-de-janeiro-urca.rating_basis: Mountain Project calls Rio “the best urban climbing destination in the world”: hundreds of multi-pitch routes right in the city with ocean views; MP itself describes only ~70 routes, while the full Zona Sul guidebook lists 283
rio-de-janeiro-urca.hazards: Heat and sun on the slabs, slippery rock after rain and fog, long runouts between bolts, muggings on some trails, sudden tropical downpours
rio-de-janeiro-urca.crowd_note: At weekends guided groups queue on the classics Via dos Italianos and K2; quiet on weekdays
rio-de-janeiro-urca.region: Rio de Janeiro, Urca neighbourhood (Praia Vermelha), Pão de Açúcar and Urca Natural Monument
rio-de-janeiro-urca.season: May–September (the southern “winter”: dry, +24…+26 °C, best friction); April and October–November are warm with occasional downpours; December–February is hot and humid (+30 °C and above on sunny slabs), so climbing happens only early in the morning and on shady walls; in Rio the season opens with the climbers' festival at Praia Vermelha
rio-de-janeiro-urca.transfer: ~30–50 min by taxi from Galeão international airport (GIG) to Urca; ~10 min from domestic Santos Dumont (SDU); city buses run to Praia Vermelha
rio-de-janeiro-urca.rock_note: solid granite-gneiss on the coastal domes of Sugarloaf (396 m), Urca and Babilônia: steep slabs and vertical faces on small edges and “scoops”, cracks and chimneys; sparsely bolted multi-pitch routes right above the ocean and the city
rio-de-janeiro-urca.approach: 10–30 min from Praia Vermelha beach along the Cláudio Coutinho tourist trail and side paths to the starts; Corcovado is ~25 min from the Paineiras road; from the top of Sugarloaf you descend by cable car
rio-de-janeiro-urca.restrictions: The Urca and Sugarloaf rocks are a protected natural area of the city (Monumento Natural dos Morros do Pão de Açúcar e da Urca): stay on the trails and leave no litter. Descend from the summit on the Bondinho cable car (a ticket up costs over 150 reais; according to climbers' reports, the ride down to Morro da Urca is free for them). There have been muggings in the past on the Corcovado and Babilônia trails — go in a group and leave valuables behind. Wet slabs after rain and fog are very slippery.
rio-de-janeiro-urca.guidebook: Guia de Escaladas da Zona Sul e das Ilhas Costeiras do Rio de Janeiro (André Ilha, Kika Bradford) — 283 routes on 11 mountains; guidebooks by Flávio Daflon and Delson de Queiroz “Urca” and “Floresta da Tijuca”
rio-de-janeiro-urca.stay: Hotels and hostels in Urca, Botafogo and Copacabana (10–20 min to Praia Vermelha by public transport or taxi)
pros: Multi-pitch climbing with ocean views right in the city
Reachable by public transport, no car needed
Dry, warm “winter” from May to September
Easy to combine with beach time and sightseeing
cons: Too hot and humid in summer
Sparse bolting — a confident leader is needed
Safety concerns on some trails
Little information in English, local Brazilian grading system
rio-de-janeiro-urca.airport: GIG — Rio de Janeiro Galeão, ~40 min; SDU — Santos Dumont, ~10 min
famous_lines: Via dos Italianos 5.10a/b (6a+), 9 pitches, Pão de Açúcar
Secundo Costa Neto 5.11 (6c+), 10 pitches, Pão de Açúcar
Luis Arnaud 5.7 (5a), 6 pitches, Morro da Babilônia
school_notes: Guides speaking English, Spanish and Portuguese; ascents of Sugarloaf and Corcovado
Guided Sugarloaf ascent for all levels, including beginners

squamish.description: A town at the foot of the Stawamus Chief granite monolith, between an ocean fjord and the mountains — Canada's crack-climbing mecca. Thousands of trad routes, from single pitches at the Smoke Bluffs to multi-pitch classics on the Apron and the Grand Wall, plus thousands of boulders in the forest and sport routes in the Cheakamus Canyon. This is where Chris Sharma climbed Dreamcatcher 9a.
squamish.rating_basis: Canada's crack-climbing mecca: ~2,800 routes and problems on Mountain Project (~19k views a month), about 3,750 on theCrag; over 3,500 boulder problems in Bourdon's guide
squamish.hazards: Bears (don't leave food out), wet slabs after rain, long multi-pitch routes with tricky descents, mosquitoes
squamish.crowd_note: In July–August there are queues on Diedre, the Apron and the Smoke Bluffs, and the Chief campground is overflowing; quieter on weekdays and at the more distant crags
squamish.region: British Columbia, Coast Mountains, 65 km north of Vancouver
squamish.season: July–September is the driest period; in May–June and October you can climb between rain spells (forest bouldering is good on cool, dry days in spring and autumn); November to March is the Pacific coast rainy season
squamish.transfer: ~1–1.5 h from Vancouver airport along the scenic Sea-to-Sky Highway; there are shuttle buses, but it's better to rent a car at the airport — rentals in Squamish cost more
squamish.rock_note: solid granite (granodiorite) on the ~700 m Stawamus Chief monolith: perfect cracks, the Apron slabs and the big walls of the Grand Wall; thousands of granite boulders in the forest at its base; sport routes in the Cheakamus Canyon
squamish.approach: 1–20 min from the campground and parking at the base of the Chief and the Smoke Bluffs, within town; 20–45 min to the upper walls and Cheakamus
squamish.restrictions: Within the District of Squamish it is forbidden to sleep outside campgrounds, including in cars and vans; on Crown land stays are limited to 14 days — watch for fire bans. Stawamus Chief Provincial Park campground costs from CAD 10 per person (no reservations, according to Mountain Project). Some crags on private land are closed to climbing.
squamish.guidebook: Squamish Select (Marc Bourdon), Climbers Guide to Squamish (Kevin McLane), Marc Bourdon's bouldering guide (2022, more than 3,500 problems)
squamish.stay: Stawamus Chief climbers' campground at the foot of the wall (1–10 min to the routes), Klahanie and Alice Lake campgrounds, hostels and motels in Squamish; wild camping in the Cheakamus Canyon
pros: Canada's best cracks and multi-pitch granite
Huge forest bouldering area next to the campground
Short approaches, everything within town
Beautiful scenery, Vancouver an hour away
cons: Rainy climate — reliably dry only in July–September
Trad skills and a rack of cams needed
Crowded in summer, strict bans on sleeping in cars
Expensive accommodation in high season
school_notes: Crack, trad and multi-pitch courses, guiding on the Chief
Trad courses and guides in Squamish and Whistler
Club courses: intro to outdoor climbing and trad progression in Squamish

magic-wood.description: A mossy spruce forest with gneiss boulders beside a mountain stream at 1,300 m — Europe's premier summer bouldering mecca. Hundreds of problems, most of them hard and athletic, with more than a hundred lines of 8A+, including Practice of the Wild 8C. It stays cool here in summer while the lowlands bake.
magic-wood.rating_basis: One of the world's best summer bouldering areas: >100 problems of 8A and harder, Sharma's Practice of the Wild; top ratings on 27crags/Mountain Project
magic-wood.hazards: Slippery mossy landings, wet rock after rain, mosquitoes, the river right next to some boulders
magic-wood.crowd_note: In July–August the campground and the classics (Kamel, Beach) are packed with an international crowd; quieter in May and October
magic-wood.season: June–September is the main season; April–May (depending on snow) and October are quieter, with good friction; in winter only for strong climbers on a few boulders
magic-wood.transfer: By car: ~2 h from Zurich on the A13 (exit 26 “Rofla / Avers-Juf / Ferrera”); by train to Thusis, then PostBus to the Ferrera, Schmelzi stop
magic-wood.rock_note: compact gneiss in a mossy spruce forest by a mountain stream: steep, athletic lines on small holds, roofs and arêtes
magic-wood.approach: 2–10 min on foot from Camping Bodhi; the whole area covers ~250 × 500 m of forest
magic-wood.restrictions: The area exists thanks to the patience of the Ferrera municipality: climb only within the marked zone and stick to the main paths; wild camping is forbidden and van overnights are allowed only at Camping Bodhi — elsewhere in the valley fines reach CHF 1,000; don't park on the village streets; use the toilets at the campground or the Edelweiss restaurant
magic-wood.guidebook: Magic Wood — Bloc (3rd edition), sold at the campground; 27crags topo
magic-wood.stay: Camping Bodhi right by the boulders (crash pad and shoe rental, cash and card accepted, no booking), Hotel Edelweiss in Ausserferrera and Alpenrose in Innerferrera
pros: Cool in summer, when the rest of Europe is too hot
A huge number of hard classic lines
Campground right by the boulders, crash pad rental
Fairy-tale forest atmosphere
cons: Few easy problems for beginners
Frequent summer rain and thunderstorms; boulders by the river are slow to dry
Packed in July–August
Strict overnight and parking rules
magic-wood.airport: ZRH — Zurich, ~2 h; MXP — Milan Malpensa, ~2.5 h
famous_lines: Practice of the Wild 8C — Chris Sharma, 2004

ticino-cresciano.description: The slopes of the Riviera valley near Bellinzona are strewn with granite-gneiss boulders — one of the world's top winter bouldering destinations. Cresciano has around 600 problems and the legendary Dreamtime 8B+ and The Story of Two Worlds 8C; further up the valley lies forested Chironico, and the neighbouring valleys hold Brione and Val Bavona.
ticino-cresciano.rating_basis: One of the world's leading winter bouldering areas: Dreamtime and The Story of Two Worlds, ~600 problems in Cresciano plus the large neighbouring areas of Chironico and Brione; UKC, madboulder, 27crags
ticino-cresciano.hazards: Highballs and uneven landings on the slope, sharp crystals, fines for parking in the wrong places
ticino-cresciano.crowd_note: Busy at Christmas and on winter weekends, especially at Filo a Sbalzo by the parking and on the 7A–8A classics
ticino-cresciano.region: Ticino, Riviera valley (Cresciano — Osogna) and Leventina (Chironico), near Bellinzona
ticino-cresciano.season: October–April; the best friction comes on cold, dry days from November to February (Cresciano), with Chironico in spring and autumn; hot in summer, apart from moderate problems in the shade
ticino-cresciano.transfer: From Milan or Zurich by car on the A2 via the Gotthard to Bellinzona, then a few minutes to Cresciano; a Swiss motorway vignette is required (~CHF 40); from Lugano by train/bus
ticino-cresciano.rock_note: light-grey, rough granite-gneiss in a chestnut forest: steep lines, arêtes, small sharp holds; boulders scattered along the slope between Cresciano and Osogna
ticino-cresciano.approach: Cresciano: leave the car in the village, ~25 min on foot to the first boulders (driving up to the boulders is forbidden); Chironico: paid parking at Chironico, Nivo and Grumo, 5–15 min from the sectors
ticino-cresciano.restrictions: Cresciano: since October 2021 the local Patriziato has banned driving and parking near the boulders — use only the parking in the village, checks are carried out; brush off tick marks. Chironico: since 2024 (the “Save the Boulders” pilot) parking is allowed only at three paid lots (CHF 0.5/h or CHF 12/day), van overnights cost an extra CHF 2 tourist tax per person, camping is not allowed. Access in the region is sensitive — violations could lead to closures
ticino-cresciano.guidebook: Ticino Bouldering / 27crags topo (Cresciano, Chironico, Brione, Val Bavona)
ticino-cresciano.stay: Hostel in Cresciano (recently reopened), guesthouses, a campground in Claro; in Chironico only paid van parking areas
pros: World-class rock with excellent winter friction
Legendary ultra-hard lines
Several areas within half an hour of each other
Sunny southern Switzerland
cons: Few easy problems
Access restrictions and paid parking
Sharp rock shreds your skin fast
Switzerland is expensive
ticino-cresciano.airport: MXP — Milan Malpensa, ~1.5 h; ZRH — Zurich, ~2 h; LUG — Lugano, ~40 min
famous_lines: Dreamtime 8B+ (Cresciano) — Fred Nicole, 2000, one of the world's first 8B+/8C
The Story of Two Worlds 8C (Cresciano) — Dave Graham

yangshuo.description: Yangshuo is a town among karst towers on the Li River and China's main sport climbing hub. More than a thousand sport routes on some 25 separate towers: from the easy slabs of Swiss Cheese to the overhanging arch of Moon Hill and 8c+ routes on White Mountain. You cycle to the crags through rice paddies.
yangshuo.rating_basis: China's main climbing hub: 1,000+ sport routes on 25+ karst towers (UKC), routes up to 8c+, well-developed infrastructure of shops and cafés
yangshuo.hazards: Heat and humidity, slippery rock in damp weather, mosquitoes; old gear and loose rock on rarely visited crags
yangshuo.crowd_note: Crowds and price hikes during Golden Week (early October); the rest of the time the crags are quiet
yangshuo.region: Guangxi, around Guilin, Li River valley
yangshuo.season: September–February; best in October–December (November is ideal); spring is damp, summer hot and rainy
yangshuo.transfer: Fly to Guilin and take a 1.5-hour bus, or a high-speed train to Yangshuo station from Guangzhou, Shenzhen or Hong Kong
yangshuo.rock_note: limestone karst towers: overhangs with tufas (Moon Hill), rounded jugs (White Mountain), small crimps (Lei Pi Shan)
yangshuo.approach: 10–30 min from town to the crags by bike or scooter, then 5–20 min on foot
yangshuo.restrictions: Check China's entry rules (visa or visa-free entry) before you travel; Moon Hill is a tourist site with an entrance fee; crowds and price hikes during Golden Week (early October)
yangshuo.guidebook: Yangshuo Rock Climbs (Tyson Wallace), updated annually, sold in Yangshuo's cafés and climbing shops
yangshuo.stay: Hostels and guesthouses in Yangshuo (Climber's Inn); for a month-long stay it pays to rent an apartment; bike and scooter rental
pros: Huge choice of routes at all levels
Cheap living, well-developed climber infrastructure
Shady and overhanging crags for hot and rainy days
Scenic karst landscape
cons: The rock “sweats” in spring; summer brings heat and downpours
Visa / entry rules to check, language and internet difficulties
The grade range at a given crag is often narrow
school_notes: Shop, rental and guides (at the Lizard Lounge café), plus a bouldering cave
Yangshuo's original climbing centre: guides, guidebook, rental
Courses and rental in central Yangshuo

suesca.description: A long sandstone cliff above a river, an hour's drive from Bogotá — the birthplace of Colombian climbing 80 years ago. Hundreds of trad and sport routes from 5.6 to 5.13, including easy multi-pitch classics, plenty of schools and guides, and a cool highland climate all year round.
suesca.rating_basis: The cradle of Colombian climbing and the country's main area: 300–500 routes depending on the source (212 on Mountain Project, >300 according to ClimbingAway), classic beginner multi-pitches close to the capital
suesca.hazards: Slippery sandstone after rain, fast-building thunderstorms, strong high-altitude sun, trains on the tracks along the trail, old protection on some trad routes
suesca.crowd_note: At weekends and on public holidays there are lots of groups from Bogotá and climbing schools, with queues on the easy classics; quiet on weekdays
suesca.region: Cundinamarca, Eastern Cordillera, ~60 km north of Bogotá
suesca.season: climbable year-round (highlands, ~+18…+20 °C by day), but the best dry windows are December–March and July–August (sometimes into September); April–May and October–November are the rainy seasons
suesca.transfer: ~1–1.5 h from Bogotá: buses from the North Terminal every 15–30 min (~$2), or by car on the Autopista Norte (2 toll booths); at weekends a tourist train runs from Sabana station
suesca.rock_note: compact quartz sandstone: a long cliff above the Bogotá River with cracks, dihedrals, roofs and slabs; multi-pitch routes of up to 5 pitches (~150 m)
suesca.approach: 5–20 min on a flat trail alongside the railway tracks and the river from the parking by Suesca village; sectors are numbered from right to left
suesca.restrictions: Park at the services near the rock, not in the village; the approach follows an active tourist railway — stay alert. For routes harder than 5.10 and multi-pitches, locals recommend ACME-certified guides. The weather changes quickly — bring a rain jacket.
suesca.guidebook: Local topos and online descriptions (Mountain Project, theCrag, the Pelecanus website); guides and topos available at the camps by the rock
suesca.stay: Climbing camps and hostels at the foot of the cliff (Caminos de Suesca — with a climbing wall, gear rental and guides; Camp Suesca, Refugio La Roca), guesthouses in the village; many people come for the day from Bogotá
pros: Lots of easy multi-pitch classics and schools for beginners
Cool “eternal spring” climate at 2,600 m
Easy bus ride from Bogotá
Gear rental and camps by the rock
cons: Two rainy seasons a year
Mostly trad, little hard sport
Crowded at weekends
Altitude of 2,600 m — the first few days can be tough
school_notes: Guided trips to Suesca from Bogotá, gear included

vinales.description: The Viñales valley, with its tobacco fields and karst hills known as “mogotes”, is the cradle of Cuban climbing. Around 230 sport routes on tropical limestone: caves with stalactites, tufas and multi-pitch routes up to 150 m, mostly in the 6a–7b range. People come here for the atmosphere and the journey rather than the number of routes.
vinales.rating_basis: Cuba's main climbing area: ~230 sport routes on Mountain Project (>200 according to ClimbingAway), unusual caves among tobacco fields; the rating is lowered by old bolts, unclear legal status and complicated logistics
vinales.hazards: Heat and humidity, rusty old bolts and anchors (check them), wasps and insects in the caves, power and phone outages across the island, hurricanes from June to November
vinales.crowd_note: Few climbers even at the height of the season; at the crags you'll mostly meet locals and a couple of foreign groups
vinales.region: Pinar del Río, Viñales valley (UNESCO site), western Cuba
vinales.season: November–April is the dry season, best December–March (+25…+28 °C); April is hot; May to October is the rainy season with heat and humidity, and June to November brings a risk of hurricanes
vinales.transfer: Fly to Havana (direct flights from Moscow available), then 2–3 h to Viñales by Viazul bus, shared colectivo taxi (~$20 per person) or private taxi (~$100)
vinales.rock_note: tropical limestone of the karst “mogote” hills: overhanging caves with stalactites and tufas, vertical pocketed walls, multi-pitch routes up to 150 m; some old bolts have been replaced with titanium ones
vinales.approach: 10–30 min on foot across the flat valley floor through tobacco fields from Viñales village or the road (taxi to the more distant crags ~$8)
vinales.restrictions: The legal status is unclear: since 2012 access to the mountains of Viñales National Park has formally been restricted to official trails with a guide, and climbing has never been officially permitted. In practice people climb openly and no foreigners have been fined, but rangers sometimes ask climbers to leave; the authorities periodically harass Cuban climbers — keep a low profile and be respectful. US citizens face restrictions on travel to Cuba. Climbing gear can't be bought on the island — bring everything you need (local climbers will welcome donations of quickdraws and ropes).
vinales.guidebook: Cuba Climbing (Armando Menocal, 2009 — Viñales only); up-to-date information on cubaclimbing.com and Mountain Project
vinales.stay: Private guesthouses (casas particulares) in Viñales village — cheap, with home cooking; hosts will help arrange taxis and guides
pros: Unusual caves and tufas amid tropical nature
Dry, warm winter
Cheap guesthouses and friendly local climbers
Visa-free for Russians, with direct flights from Moscow
cons: Unclear legal status of climbing in the national park
Old bolts on some routes
No gear shops, difficulties with money and connectivity
Not many routes, few hard ones
famous_lines: Wasp Factory 5.12c (7b+), Cueva Cabeza de Vaca
school_notes: Speaks English and Spanish; a day with a guide and gear ~$40–50

frankenjura.description: The hilly, wooded Franconian Switzerland, with a thousand limestone crags, is one of the densest sport climbing areas in the world. Short, powerful routes on pockets, the history of the redpoint and Güllich's legendary Action Directe. In summer the forest shade saves the day, and after climbing there are Franconian beer gardens.
frankenjura.rating_basis: The historic birthplace of the redpoint (Kurt Albert) and of Güllich's Action Directe: ~7,000 routes on ~1,000 crags, a huge number of 8a+ and harder; UKC, Mountain Project, theCrag
frankenjura.hazards: Polish on the classics, sparse protection on easy old routes, ticks in the forest
frankenjura.crowd_note: At weekends the popular crags (Weißenstein, Roter Fels, Krottenseer Turm) are busy with locals and polished; on weekdays and at more remote crags it's quiet
frankenjura.region: Bavaria, Franconian Switzerland (Obertrubach, Pottenstein), between Nuremberg and Bayreuth
frankenjura.season: late March–October; best April–June and September–October; in summer, north-facing walls in the forest (muggy in August); in winter, only the occasional dry, sunny day
frankenjura.transfer: A car is essential: Nuremberg ~40–50 min, Munich ~2 h, Frankfurt ~3 h; public transport doesn't reach the crags
frankenjura.rock_note: grey dolomitic limestone in the forest: short (8–30 m), powerful routes on pockets — from slabs to overhangs, on ~1,000 individual crags and towers
frankenjura.approach: 5–20 min through the forest from parking by the villages; the crags are spread over a large area, so you need a car
frankenjura.restrictions: The nature park's “Kletterkonzeption” (climbing plan) applies: zone 1 — climbing prohibited; zone 2 — existing routes only, up to the anchor, no new routes; zone 3 — new routes allowed away from vegetation; zones are marked with signs at the crags. In spring some crags close for the nesting of protected birds — see the current list on the IG Klettern and DAV Felsinfo websites. Don't toprope directly through the anchor; by tacit agreement, no bouldering guidebooks are published
frankenjura.guidebook: Kletterführer Frankenjura, volumes 1 and 2 (Panico) — >7,000 routes on ~1,000 crags; the frankenjura.com database
frankenjura.stay: Gasthof Eichler with its camping meadow in Obertrubach, campgrounds in Betzenstein, Auerbach and Königstein, Kormershof in Allersdorf; guesthouses with beer gardens in the villages
pros: Huge density of crags and routes
Forest shade — climbable in summer
A world centre of hard climbing
Beer gardens and cosy villages
cons: Short, stiff, powerful routes; old grades are harsh
Sparse protection on easy old routes, nuts needed
Winter is off-season, rain in November
Car needed
frankenjura.airport: NUE — Nuremberg, ~45 min; MUC — Munich, ~2 h
famous_lines: Action Directe 9a / UIAA 11 (Waldkopf) — Wolfgang Güllich, 1991, the world's first 9a
school_notes: Outdoor courses for children and adults
Mountain sports school, climbing courses
Courses and guiding in the heart of the area

albarracin.description: Thousands of red sandstone boulders in a pine forest next to the medieval town of Albarracín at ~1,200 m. Most problems are 6A–7B — steep roofs and arêtes with mantel top-outs — with plenty of options for beginners. The area is protected (rock art, birds), so strict rules apply.
albarracin.rating_basis: Spain's main bouldering area: >2,300 problems on red sandstone, mostly 6A–7B; high ratings on UKC/theCrag
albarracin.hazards: Highballs with uneven landings, fragile wet sandstone, fines for breaking the regulations
albarracin.crowd_note: In spring and autumn the Parking, Arrastradero and Techos sectors get crowded at weekends and on holidays, with a queue at Techo Don Pepo
albarracin.region: Aragon, Teruel, Pinares de Rodeno Protected Landscape
albarracin.season: spring and autumn are best (March–May, October–November); cold in winter but with excellent friction and occasional light snow; hot in summer
albarracin.transfer: By car only: Valencia ~2 h, Zaragoza ~2.5 h, Madrid ~3–3.5 h
albarracin.rock_note: fine-grained red sandstone (rodeno) in a pine forest: steep boulders with mantel top-outs, roofs, arêtes; boulders from 1 to 20 m high
albarracin.approach: 1–30 min from the parking areas along the Albarracín — Dornaque forest road; parking is paid (blue zone)
albarracin.restrictions: Strict regulation by the Government of Aragon: climb only in the marked zones; the Peninsula, Valle de la Madera, Mirador and Psicokiller sectors are closed from 10 January to 15 August (bird nesting); no climbing on boulders visible from the paved road, within 30 m of rock art or on painted boulders; night climbing is prohibited (climbing is allowed only from an hour before sunrise to an hour after sunset), as are bolts, new sectors, camping and fires; campervan overnights only at the La Escombrera car park and by the Dornaque centre; use minimal chalk, brush the holds, don't climb on wet sandstone
albarracin.guidebook: Albarracín Bouldering (Palmer, 2021: >2,300 problems in 21 sectors + >600 in Bezas), albarracinbouldering.com
albarracin.stay: Camping Ciudad de Albarracín (tents and bungalows, ~4 km from the boulders), Sandstone guesthouse (popular with climbers, crash pad rental), hotels and apartments in the medieval town
pros: Huge choice of problems from 5 to 7B
Beautiful forest with a medieval town nearby
Good for beginners and groups
The altitude keeps the heat off in spring and autumn
cons: Strict rules and closed sectors
After rain you have to wait for the sandstone to dry
Cold in winter, hot in summer
Car needed
albarracin.airport: VLC — Valencia, ~2 h; ZAZ — Zaragoza, ~2.5 h; MAD — Madrid, ~3.5 h
famous_lines: Techo Don Pepo 7A (Techos) — the most popular boulder in the forest
La Lágrima 6C+ — on the guidebook cover

chulilla.description: A white village above the Turia river canyon and one of Europe's best winter sport climbing areas. Walls on both sides of the gorge let you choose sun or shade, and long 30–40 m endurance routes make it a paradise for the 7a–8a range. Everything is within walking distance of the village.
chulilla.rating_basis: One of Europe's top winter sport climbing areas: >1,400 routes, thousands of quality 7a–8a lines in a canyon with a choice of sun or shade; UKC's “Euro Sport Climbing Destination” series, PlanetMountain
chulilla.hazards: Rockfall in the canyon (there has been a well-known major collapse), polish, long routes — check your rope length (80–100 m ropes are sometimes needed)
chulilla.crowd_note: At Christmas, New Year and Easter the village is packed with climbers and there are queues on popular sectors; quieter on weekdays
chulilla.region: Valencian Community, Los Serranos comarca, Turia river gorge
chulilla.season: October–April; best November–March (13–17 °C, sunny), hard routes December–February; hot and greasy in summer
chulilla.transfer: ~1 h by car from Valencia (CV-35, then CV-395); Hispano Chelvana bus on weekdays, with the stop to be requested in advance; no car needed in the village
chulilla.rock_note: grey-orange limestone of the Turia canyon: long vertical and slightly overhanging 30–40 m endurance routes with bouldery starts, tufa-like “sinters” on Pared de Enfrente
chulilla.approach: 10–25 min on foot from the village along trails through the canyon; no car needed in the village
chulilla.restrictions: Wild camping is prohibited (campervans unofficially park at the car parks at the village entrances, without facilities); Leave No Trace — no fires, pack out your rubbish
chulilla.guidebook: Chulilla (2025, >1,400 routes, 59 sectors), topos also on climbmaps.com
chulilla.stay: El Altico climbers' refugio (≈€15 a night, climbing wall, pool, van parking), apartments and rooms in the village from ~€25; Goscanos climbers' bar, Al Coxinillo gear shop
pros: Huge number of quality 6c–8a routes
Warm, dry winter
Everything within walking distance of the village, a convenient refugio
Choice of sun or shade in the canyon
cons: Limited choice for beginners
Polished holds on popular classics
Too hot in summer
Crowded during holidays
chulilla.airport: VLC — Valencia, ~1 h; ALC — Alicante, ~2.5–3 h
school_notes: Adventure tourism in Chulilla, including climbing
Beginner session
British guides, week-long sport climbing trip

costa-blanca-sella.description: The Sella valley is the heart of the Costa Blanca, one of Europe's most popular winter destinations. Hundreds of well-bolted 4–6c routes on technical slabs and walls make it ideal for beginners and intermediates, with the multi-pitches of Puig Campana and the Peñón de Ifach and the Toix sea cliffs close by. Warm winters, cheap flights and plenty of accommodation.
costa-blanca-sella.rating_basis: The largest and most popular area on the Costa Blanca (≈500 routes) with loads of quality grade 5–6 climbing; the BMC lists it among Spain's top 5 areas for intermediate climbers
costa-blanca-sella.hazards: Polish on the classics, heat, lorries on the access road
costa-blanca-sella.crowd_note: On winter weekends and during British school holidays the popular sectors are taken over by groups, but there's plenty of choice
costa-blanca-sella.region: Valencian Community, Alicante province, Sella valley (near Puig Campana, Peñón de Ifach, Toix)
costa-blanca-sella.season: October–April is the classic “winter sun” season; in May–June and September, the north-facing Pared de Rosalía; hot in summer
costa-blanca-sella.transfer: Alicante airport, then by car: ~50–60 min to Sella (AP-7 to Villajoyosa, then ~20 km inland); car hire is cheap
costa-blanca-sella.rock_note: grey limestone: technical slabs and slabby walls in the central part, long routes on the north-facing Pared de Rosalía, steep tufas in Hidden Valley, long trad routes on El Divino
costa-blanca-sella.approach: 5–20 min from the parking areas along the dirt road beyond the Sella refugio; lorries use the road on weekdays — park completely off the track
costa-blanca-sella.restrictions: Soft limestone: clean your shoes, don't run the rope directly through the anchors, brush off tick marks. In the neighbouring Costa Blanca natural areas (Serra Gelada, Peñón de Ifach and others) the FEMECV federation publishes seasonal nesting restrictions — check before your trip
costa-blanca-sella.guidebook: Costa Blanca Climbs (>4,000 routes, 56 crags), Rockfax Costa Blanca (>4,800 routes, 50 crags); a free mini-guide to Sella's new sectors from The Orange House
costa-blanca-sella.stay: The Sella refugio at the start of the valley, The Orange House climbers' house (Finestrat, ~35 min from the airport), villas and apartments in Finestrat, Benidorm and Calpe
pros: Ideal for beginners and the 5–6c range
Warm, sunny winters by the sea
Lots of schools and guides
Puig Campana and Peñón de Ifach multi-pitches nearby
cons: Few hard routes compared with Catalonia
The central part gets little sun on winter mornings
Hot in summer
Dirt road and lorries on weekdays
